questions.question:
Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form
[latex]\forall x\left [P(x)\Rightarrow \exists yQ(x,y) \right ] [/latex]
where [latex]P[/latex] is a statement about integers, and [latex]Q[/latex] is a statement about pairs of integers. Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha's conjecture?
questions.explanation:
Conjecture: for every x with P(x), some y makes Q(x, y) true.

- Option 1 talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.
- Option 2: Q holds for all x and y, so for any x any y works [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 3: one fixed y works for every x with P(x), so such a y exists for each x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 4 again talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.question: Let x and Y be finite sets and f:x[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Y be a function. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cup[/latex]B)|=|f(A)|+|f(B)|
options.B: For any subsets A and B of x, f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B) =f(A)[latex]\cap[/latex]f(B)
options.C: For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B)| = min{|f (A)| ,|f(B)|}
options.D: For any subsets S and T of Y, [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1 fails when f(A) and f(B) overlap.
- Option 2 fails for non-injective f: A = {1}, B = {2}, f(1) = f(2) = y gives [latex]f(A\cap B)=\emptyset[/latex] but [latex]f(A)\cap f(B)=\{y\}[/latex].
- Option 3 fails for the same example.
- Option 4: [latex]x\in f^{-1}(S\cap T)\iff f(x)\in S[/latex] and [latex]f(x)\in T\iff x\in f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always true.

Answer: [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the following experiment.
Step 1. Flip a fair coin twice.
Step 2. If the outcomes are(TAILS, HEADS) then output Y and stop.
Step 3. If the outcomes are either(HEADS, HEADS) or(HEADS, TAILS), then output N and stop.
Step 4. If the out comes are(TAILS, TAILS), then go to Step1.
The probability that the output of the experiment is Y is (up to two decimal places)_____.
questions.explanation:
In each round of two flips: Y with probability 1/4 (TH), N with 1/2 (HH or HT), repeat with 1/4 (TT).

[latex]P(Y)=\frac{1/4}{1/4+1/2}=\frac13\approx0.33[/latex]

Answer: 0.33

questions.question:
Let [latex]G[/latex] be a simple, finite, undirected graph with vertex set [latex] \{v_1,...,v_n\}[/latex]. Let [latex] \Delta (G)[/latex] denote the maximum degree of [latex]G[/latex] and let [latex] N=\{1,2,...\} [/latex] denote the set of all possible colors. Color the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] using the following greedy strategy: for [latex]i = 1,...,n[/latex]
[latex]color(v_i)\leftarrow min\{ j \in N: \text{ no neighbour of } v_i \text{ is colored } j\}[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of [latex]G[/latex].
options.B: The number of colors used is at most [latex] \Delta (G)+1[/latex].
options.C: The number of colors used is at most[latex] \Delta (G)[/latex].
options.D: The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of [latex]G[/latex].

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Each vertex gets the smallest colour not used by any neighbour, so no edge joins equal colours [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] proper colouring [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A vertex has at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex] neighbours, so among colours [latex]1\ldots\Delta+1[/latex] one is always free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] at most [latex]\Delta(G)+1[/latex] colours [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]K_n[/latex] needs n = [latex]\Delta+1[/latex] colours, so "at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex]" is FALSE.
- A bad vertex order can use more colours than the chromatic number (e.g. on some bipartite graphs) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.question:
Consider the first order predicate formula:
[latex]\forall x[\forall z\; z|x\Rightarrow ((z=x)\vee (z=1))\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\exists w(w> x)\wedge (\forall z \; z|w\Rightarrow ((w=z)\vee (z=1)))][/latex]
Here 'a|b' denotes that 'a divides b', where a and b are integers. Consider the following sets:

S1: {1, 2, 3, ..., 100}
S2: Set of all positive integers
S3: Set of all integers
Which of the above sets satisfy [latex]\varphi[/latex] ?
questions.explanation:
The formula says: for every x that is prime (only divisors are 1 and x), there is a larger prime w. In other words, there is no largest prime.

- S1 = {1, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 100}: 97 is prime, but no prime larger than 97 is in S1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fails.
- S2, S3: there are infinitely many primes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] satisfied.

Answer: S2 and S3

questions.question: In a connected graph, a bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects a graph. Which one of the following statements is true?

options.B: A bridge cannot be part of a simple cycle
options.C: Every edge of a clique with size [latex]\geq[/latex] 3 is a bridge (A clique is any complete subgraph of a graph)
options.D: A graph with bridges cannot have a cycle

questions.explanation:
If an edge were on a cycle, the rest of the cycle would still connect its ends after removing it, so it would not be a bridge.

- Every edge of a tree is a bridge.
- Clique edges (size [latex]\ge[/latex] 3) lie on triangles, so they are not bridges.
- A graph can have both bridges and cycles.

Answer: A bridge cannot be part of a simple cycle

questions.question: Consider the operators [latex] \diamond [/latex] and [latex] \square [/latex] defined by [latex] a \diamond b=a+2 b, a \square b=a b [/latex], for positive integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.C: Operator [latex] \diamond [/latex] over the operator [latex] \square [/latex] obeys the distributive law
options.D: Operator [latex] \square [/latex] over the operator [latex] \diamond [/latex] obeys the distributive law

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]\diamond[/latex] associative? [latex](a\diamond b)\diamond c=a+2b+2c[/latex], [latex]a\diamond(b\diamond c)=a+2b+4c[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NO.
- [latex]\square[/latex] is ordinary multiplication [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] associative, YES.
- [latex]\diamond[/latex] over [latex]\square[/latex]: [latex]a\diamond(b\square c)=a+2bc[/latex], but [latex](a\diamond b)\square(a\diamond c)=(a+2b)(a+2c)[/latex]. For [latex]a=b=c=1[/latex]: 3 vs 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NO.
- [latex]\square[/latex] over [latex]\diamond[/latex]: [latex]a\square(b\diamond c)=a(b+2c)=ab+2ac=(a\square b)\diamond(a\square c)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] YES.

Answer: [latex]\square[/latex] is associative; [latex]\square[/latex] distributes over [latex]\diamond[/latex]

questions.question: Let R be a relation on the set of ordered pairs of positive integers such that [latex]((p,q),(r,s)) \in R[/latex] if and only if [latex]p-s=q-r[/latex]. Which one of the following is true about R?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Reflexive needs p [latex]-[/latex] q = q [latex]-[/latex] p, i.e. p = q. Fails for (1, 2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not reflexive.
- Symmetric: ((r,s),(p,q)) needs r [latex]-[/latex] q = s [latex]-[/latex] p, which rearranges to p [latex]-[/latex] s = q [latex]-[/latex] r [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] symmetric.

Answer: Not reflexive but symmetric

questions.question: Which one of the following well formed formulae is a tautology?

options.B: [latex](\forall x[\exists yR(x,y)\rightarrow S(x,y)])\rightarrow \forall x\exists y S(x,y)[/latex]
options.C: [latex][\forall x\exists yP(x,y)\rightarrow R(x,y)]\leftrightarrow [\forall x\exists y(\neg P(x,y))\vee R(x,y)][/latex]
options.D: [latex]\forall x \forall y P(x,y) \rightarrow \forall x\forall y P(y,x)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Option 3: [latex]P\rightarrow R\equiv\neg P\vee R[/latex], and both sides apply the same quantifiers to equivalent formulas [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] tautology.

- Option 1: [latex]\forall x\exists y[/latex] does not imply [latex]\exists y\forall x[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not a tautology.
- Option 2: fails, e.g. when nothing satisfies R.

Note: option 4 is also logically valid (the bound variables are only renamed). The official key is option 3.

Answer: Option 3
